opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that he really doesn't carry himself like a legend. You'd expect someone with a Turing Award, someone who basically helped invent convolutional networks, to be a bit distant or guarded. But with Yann it's the opposite. He's very direct and very open, and he'll happily argue with you about an idea as if you're on equal footing. He doesn't pull rank in a discussion. If you have a good point, he engages with it; if he thinks you're wrong, he tells you, and he expects you to push back on him too.

He's also genuinely curious. Even now he gets excited about research ideas the way a grad student does. When you talk to him about world models, self-supervised learning, or why he thinks autoregressive LLMs aren't the full answer, you can feel he still really cares about the science, not about status or winning a debate for its own sake.

And there's a human side people don't always see. He has lots of interests outside AI: music, building things, sailing, technology in general. So conversations with him don't feel like meetings with an authority figure. They feel like talking with a very smart, slightly stubborn, fun colleague who happens to have been right about a lot of things for a long time.

I think that's part of why young researchers like being around him. He treats ideas as what matters, not seniority, and that makes him feel approachable.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, the first time I really interacted with Yann was when I was still a PhD student, and I remember being nervous because, come on, it's Yann LeCun. But within a few minutes it just felt like talking to a colleague. He doesn't perform his status at all. He's genuinely curious, he asks you questions about your work, and he actually listens to the answer.

I think part of it is that he's still a researcher at heart. He's not someone who stopped thinking about the technical details twenty years ago and now just gives talks. He'll argue with you about an architecture, he'll push back on your intuitions, and he fully expects you to push back on his. And he's wrong sometimes! He'll admit it. That makes a huge difference. If someone that senior is willing to be wrong in front of you, it gives you permission to think out loud too.

And honestly, he's just very direct. There's no layer of politics or diplomacy you have to decode. If he thinks an idea is bad, he says so. If he thinks it's good, he gets excited like a grad student. When I was working on ConvNeXt, he was one of the people who really cared about the question of whether ConvNets still had a place, and you could tell it wasn't about ego, it was about the science. He wanted to know the answer.

So I think the approachability comes from the fact that he's never really left the lab. He's a famous person, but he's a famous person who still reads papers, still has strong opinions about loss functions, and still enjoys a good argument at the whiteboard.
